title: OTP, concurrency and performance
intro: Start with functions. Add processes for state ownership, concurrency or lifecycle. Choose shared storage by its read/write pattern; measure before changing the architecture.
status: Built-in Elixir and Erlang tools need no extra package. Follow the installed Elixir/OTP documentation; node-local memory and supervision do not provide durable storage.

items.when: The work is business logic or a transformation that needs no independent lifecycle.
items.boundary: Keep it in functions. Adding a process adds messaging and coordination costs; it does not make a function faster.

items.when: A file or collection should be processed incrementally, without building every intermediate result in memory.
items.boundary: Streams are lazy: enumerate them to run the work. They are not parallel; collecting all results can still exhaust memory.

items.when: Short-lived work can run alongside its caller, such as fetching independent inputs.
items.boundary: Task.async links failures to the caller. Await the result and define timeout/cleanup behavior. Tasks do not survive node restarts as durable jobs.

items.when: Tasks need an application-owned supervisor or must fail independently of the requesting process.
items.boundary: async still links to the caller; choose async_nolink when isolation is required and handle results/exits. max_children rejects excess starts; it is not a waiting queue or a rate limiter.

items.when: Independent items can be processed concurrently with a bounded number of tasks.
items.boundary: Enumerate the stream; set concurrency and timeout policy. ordered: false avoids buffering for input order when order is unnecessary. Task.Supervisor.async_stream_nolink adds supervised, unlinked task execution.

items.when: One process needs to hold a small value accessed through get/update functions.
items.boundary: This is Elixir Agent, not an AI agent. Operations run serially inside its process. Choose GenServer for messages, timers or a richer lifecycle; ETS for concurrent table access.

items.when: A long-lived process owns state or coordinates a resource, for example a connection or session.
items.boundary: Callbacks execute serially. Keep slow work out of callbacks when responsiveness matters; call timeouts do not cancel server work. In-memory state needs a separate persistence strategy.

items.when: A protocol or connection has distinct states, state-specific events and transition/timeout rules.
items.boundary: Use functions or a data model for ordinary business statuses. The behaviour models a running process; supervision does not make its state durable.

items.when: Long-running children must start in order and recover according to their dependencies.
items.boundary: Choose restart and shutdown policies deliberately. Restarts do not restore lost state, and terminate callbacks are not a durability guarantee. Slow child initialization delays later children.

items.when: The application starts and stops workers as demand changes, such as one worker per active room.
items.boundary: Use Registry for discovery. A restarted supervisor does not remember the former dynamic child set; reconcile it from an authoritative source when required.

items.when: Processes need names based on runtime keys, such as tenant/session IDs, or local duplicate-key dispatch.
items.boundary: Use :via tuples rather than creating atoms from user input. Registry is node-local; it is neither cluster discovery nor durable storage.

items.when: Measurements show one process, such as a DynamicSupervisor or Task.Supervisor, bottlenecking concurrent starts.
items.boundary: Route work across partitioned children. This reduces contention in that layer; it does not parallelize a single worker or distribute work across nodes.

items.when: A process must observe another process exiting or receive a delayed message.
items.boundary: Monitors report DOWN without coupling failures; links couple lifecycles. Process.send_after schedules a message, not a durable job. Account for stale timer messages and mailbox growth.

items.when: A running server has unexpected state, memory growth or a growing mailbox.
items.boundary: Use :sys for OTP process state and bounded debugging; Process.info reports process memory and queue length. Inspecting full state can expose sensitive values and allocate large results. These tools diagnose behavior; they do not repair it.

items.when: Many processes need concurrent lookups or updates to node-local in-memory data.
items.boundary: Choose table type, ownership and access rights. Tune read/write concurrency against measurements. The table normally dies with its owner; TTL, invalidation and durability are separate.

items.when: Many processes repeatedly read a value that changes rarely, such as a static lookup or a stable resource reference. A stable :counters reference can be stored once while the counter array itself is updated.
items.boundary: Reads avoid locks and copying the value onto the caller heap. Writes copy the key table; replacing/deleting complex terms triggers a node-wide GC scan. Avoid request-time updates and expiring caches. Persistent means VM lifetime, not disk durability.

items.when: Many processes update numeric metrics without routing each increment through one server.
items.boundary: write_concurrency favors add/sub throughput with weaker read consistency. Choose atomics mode when those semantics do not fit. Fixed-width integers wrap; this is node-local memory, not an accounting ledger.

items.when: An integer operation needs an atomic result or compare-and-exchange, such as claiming a numeric slot.
items.boundary: Individual operations are atomic and mutually ordered. A sequence of operations is not a transaction. Integers wrap on overflow, and these values are not cluster-wide.

items.when: A process holds a FIFO buffer and repeated list appends would be costly.
items.boundary: A queue is a data structure, not a worker, backpressure mechanism or persistent job system. Bound its size and define overload behavior.

items.when: Output combines many byte fragments and its destination accepts iodata.
items.boundary: Keep binaries and byte lists nested until a binary is required. Avoid repeated copying; benchmark the actual construction because BEAM binary appends can also be optimized.

items.when: Small slices of large payloads live in process state or another long-lived store.
items.boundary: Inspect referenced_byte_size. Copy selected retained slices when they pin a much larger binary; copying every binary adds allocation and work.

notes.title: Choose durability separately
notes.body: Use Task for disposable work and Oban for application jobs that need persistence and retries. GenStage and Broadway regulate ingestion; source acknowledgements and retry-safe handlers determine delivery behavior.

notes.title: Measure the limiting resource
notes.body: Track latency, throughput, memory, mailbox growth, database queries and pool waits on representative traffic. Extra tasks can overload a database or an upstream API. Use Benchee for code comparisons and profilers to find where work accumulates.

notes.title: Stream database exports deliberately
notes.body: Use Ecto.Repo.stream for incremental row processing when the adapter supports it. SQL adapters require enumeration inside a transaction. Long streams occupy a database connection; batching and collecting results can change memory use.
